# Introduction

Cell-cell communication tools such as
[CellChat](https://github.com/jinworks/CellChat) start with the same
pre-processing:

1. restrict the expression data to genes in a ligand-receptor (L-R) database,
2. find genes over-expressed in each cell group (one Wilcoxon test per gene
   and per group), and
3. keep the L-R interactions whose ligand or receptor is over-expressed.

Step 2 dominates the run time on large datasets, because the number of tests
grows with genes × cell groups and they run one at a time in R.
`r Biocpkg("cellchatr")` implements these steps in Rust and runs the tests in
parallel on all CPU cores.

**Intended users.** Analysts working with single-cell RNA-seq data in
`r Biocpkg("SingleCellExperiment")` or `r Biocpkg("SummarizedExperiment")`
objects who want to find over-expressed L-R interactions between cell
groups, either as a quick standalone screen or as a faster pre-filter before
a full communication analysis.

**Relationship to CellChat.** `r Biocpkg("cellchatr")` does **not** depend on
CellChat and does not use CellChat objects. It takes any L-R table with
`ligand`, `receptor` and `interaction_name` columns. The `interaction` table
of `CellChatDB.human` / `CellChatDB.mouse` has exactly this layout, so
CellChat users can pass it in directly (see
[Using CellChatDB](#using-cellchatdb)), but CellChat is only an optional
source of an L-R database. It is not listed in `DESCRIPTION` because it is
distributed only through GitHub, which Bioconductor does not allow as a
dependency.

# Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("cellchatr")
```

Binary packages do not need Rust. Building from source requires `cargo` and
`rustc` (see `SystemRequirements` in `DESCRIPTION`).

# Example with a SingleCellExperiment

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(cellchatr)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
```

## A small ligand-receptor table

```{r lrdb}
lrdb <- data.frame(
    interaction_name = c("TGFB1_TGFBR1", "VEGFA_FLT1", "CXCL12_CXCR4",
                         "IL6_IL6R", "TNF_TNFRSF1A", "MIF_CD74",
                         "CCL2_CCR2", "PDGFB_PDGFRB", "EGF_EGFR",
                         "FGF2_FGFR1"),
    ligand = c("TGFB1", "VEGFA", "CXCL12", "IL6", "TNF",
               "MIF", "CCL2", "PDGFB", "EGF", "FGF2"),
    receptor = c("TGFBR1", "FLT1", "CXCR4", "IL6R", "TNFRSF1A",
                 "CD74", "CCR2", "PDGFRB", "EGFR", "FGFR1"),
    pathway_name = c("TGFb", "VEGF", "CXCL", "IL6", "TNF",
                     "MIF", "CCL", "PDGF", "EGF", "FGF")
)
lrdb
```

## Simulated data

We simulate log-normalized expression for 2,000 genes in 300 cells from
three cell types. TGFB1 and PDGFB are made higher in fibroblasts, and FLT1
higher in endothelial cells.

```{r sce}
set.seed(42)
genes <- unique(c(lrdb$ligand, lrdb$receptor, paste0("GENE", 1:2000)))
cell_type <- rep(c("Fibroblast", "Macrophage", "Endothelial"), each = 100)

mat <- matrix(rnorm(length(genes) * length(cell_type), mean = 1, sd = 1),
              nrow = length(genes),
              dimnames = list(genes, paste0("cell", seq_along(cell_type))))
mat[c("TGFB1", "PDGFB"), cell_type == "Fibroblast"] <-
    mat[c("TGFB1", "PDGFB"), cell_type == "Fibroblast"] + 3
mat["FLT1", cell_type == "Endothelial"] <-
    mat["FLT1", cell_type == "Endothelial"] + 3

sce <- SingleCellExperiment(
    assays = list(logcounts = mat),
    colData = DataFrame(cell_type = cell_type)
)
sce
```

## One-call workflow

`identifyInteractions()` restricts the data to L-R genes, tests every gene
in every cell type, and returns the matching interactions as a
`DataFrame`. No multiple-testing correction is applied, so we use a strict
p-value cutoff:

```{r identify}
res <- identifyInteractions(sce, lrdb, labels = "cell_type",
                            assay.type = "logcounts",
                            pval_threshold = 1e-6)
res
metadata(res)$overexpressed
```

## Step by step

The steps can also be run separately:

```{r steps}
oe <- findOverexpressedGenes(sce, labels = "cell_type", lrdb = lrdb,
                             pval_threshold = 1e-6)
oe
matchLRPairs(oe, lrdb)
```

`findOverexpressedGenes()` also accepts a plain or sparse matrix with gene
names as row names:

```{r matrix}
findOverexpressedGenes(Matrix::Matrix(mat, sparse = TRUE),
                       labels = cell_type, lrdb = lrdb,
                       pval_threshold = 1e-6)
```

# Using CellChatDB {#using-cellchatdb}

If CellChat is installed, its database can be used as-is:

```{r cellchatdb, eval = FALSE}
library(CellChat)
res <- identifyInteractions(sce, CellChatDB.human$interaction,
                            labels = "cell_type")
```

Ligands and receptors are matched by name. CellChatDB entries that refer to
multi-subunit complexes are only matched if the complex name itself is
among the over-expressed genes.

# Statistical details

For each gene and each cell group, a one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test
compares the cells in the group against all other cells (alternative:
higher in the group). P-values use the normal approximation with
tie-corrected variance and no continuity correction, matching
`wilcox.test(x, y, alternative = "greater", exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE)`:

```{r compare}
x <- mat["TGFB1", cell_type == "Fibroblast"]
y <- mat["TGFB1", cell_type != "Fibroblast"]
wilcox.test(x, y, alternative = "greater",
            exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE)$p.value
```

A gene is reported if its p-value is below `pval_threshold` in at least one
group. No multiple-testing correction is applied.

# Performance

The low-level functions `rust_subset_genes()`, `rust_wilcoxon_filter()` and
`rust_match_lr_pairs()` work on plain vectors and matrices. Here we compare
`rust_wilcoxon_filter()` with an equivalent loop over `wilcox.test()`:

```{r benchmark}
set.seed(42)
n_genes <- 500
labels_bm <- rep(c("A", "B"), each = 100)
counts_bm <- matrix(rnorm(n_genes * 200), nrow = n_genes)
gene_names <- paste0("GENE", seq_len(n_genes))

r_wilcoxon <- function(counts, labels, gene_names, pval_threshold) {
    hit <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(counts)), function(g) {
        any(vapply(unique(labels), function(ct) {
            wilcox.test(counts[g, labels == ct], counts[g, labels != ct],
                        alternative = "greater", exact = FALSE,
                        correct = FALSE)$p.value < pval_threshold
        }, logical(1)))
    }, logical(1))
    gene_names[hit]
}

t_rust <- system.time(
    rust_res <- rust_wilcoxon_filter(counts_bm, labels_bm, gene_names, 0.05)
)
t_r <- system.time(
    r_res <- r_wilcoxon(counts_bm, labels_bm, gene_names, 0.05)
)
identical(sort(rust_res), sort(r_res))
c(rust = t_rust[["elapsed"]], base_r = t_r[["elapsed"]])
```

Speed-ups depend on the number of CPU cores and grow with the number of
genes and cell groups. For the simple lookups (`rust_subset_genes()`,
`rust_match_lr_pairs()`), base R's `%in%` is already fast, and the Rust
versions are provided mainly so the whole workflow runs in one place.
